claimBoundary: This is one provenance-bound Codex pass. It is single-model evidence, not human, instructor, independent, classroom, or multi-judge validation.

claims: A monopoly is a market with a single seller of a product that has no close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry.
Unlike a price-taking competitive firm, a monopoly is a price maker: it can raise price by restricting the quantity it sells.
Because it produces less and charges more than a competitive market, a monopoly creates deadweight loss.

artifact.q: Which characteristic defines a market structure where a single seller offers a product with no close substitutes and possesses barriers to entry?
op: A price maker
A price taker
A firm with private costs
A firm with external costs
artifact.ex: A single seller of a product that has no close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry.

artifact.q: Which description best matches a monopoly?
op: A market with a single seller of a product that has no close substitutes, protected by barriers
A market with many sellers offering close substitutes and no entry barriers
A firm that can only accept the market price and cannot influence it
A buyer-controlled market where firms must lower price to sell any output
artifact.ex: Correct: it has one seller, no close substitutes, and entry barriers. A monopoly is not just any large firm.

claims: An externality is a cost or benefit from a transaction that falls on a third party who is not part of the exchange.
With a negative externality like pollution, the market produces more than the socially efficient quantity because the price excludes the spillover cost.
Correcting an externality means making decision-makers face the costs or benefits the market boundary leaves out.

artifact.df: A cost or benefit from a transaction that lands on someone outside the exchange.
artifact.eg: A factory's smoke raises nearby residents' cleanup expenses even though they did not buy the factory's output.
artifact.mi: It is just the same as any direct payment between the two traders.
artifact.cx: The extra effect is outside the bargain, so it is not part of the buyer-seller exchange itself.

artifact.tr: Cost or benefit from a transaction falling on a third party
artifact.df: This is a cost or benefit from a transaction that falls on a third party who is not part of the exchange.
artifact.eg: When a factory pollutes a nearby river, the cost of the pollution falls on the local community who do not participate in the factory's transaction.
artifact.mi: This term refers to the internal cost incurred by the producer of a good.
artifact.cx: This concept describes an external cost or benefit that affects someone outside the direct trade.

claims: A beat is a regularly recurring pulse, and meter organizes recurring beats into groups while rhythm places durations and attacks within that framework.
Duple meter groups beats in twos, triple meter groups them in threes, and quadruple meter groups them in fours.
In simple meter, each beat divides into two equal parts; in compound meter, each beat divides into three equal parts.
In a simple-meter time signature, the top number gives the beats per measure and the bottom number identifies the note value used as the beat unit.
A measure contains one recurring beat group, and bar lines separate adjacent measures in notation.
attribution: Open Music Theory by Mark Gotham, Kyle Gullings, Chelsey Hamm, Bryn Hughes, Brian Jarvis, Megan Lavengood, John Peterson, and contributors

artifact.q: In a compound meter, how is each beat divided?
op: Into two equal parts
Into three equal parts
Into four equal parts
Into one equal part
artifact.ex: Each beat in compound meter divides into three equal parts because in simple meter, each beat divides into two equal parts, and compound meter is the opposite.

op: Each beat divides into two equal parts
Each beat divides into three equal parts
Beats are grouped in threes
Measures are marked by recurring pulse
artifact.ex: Each beat divides into two equal parts in simple meter. The usual mistake is to confuse beat division with beat grouping; grouping in threes describes triple meter, not simple meter.

claims: A producer has a comparative advantage in the good it can make at the lower opportunity cost, even if another producer is better at making everything.
When each producer specializes according to comparative advantage and then trades, total output rises and both can consume beyond what they could produce alone.
Gains from trade come from differences in opportunity cost, not from absolute skill.

artifact.q: What is the primary source of gains from trade?
op: differences in opportunity cost
absolute skill
firm size
private cost
artifact.ex: Gains from trade come from differences in opportunity cost.

artifact.q: Two classmates can each produce both essays and slides, but one gives up fewer essays to make a slide deck. Which conclusion is supported?
op: That classmate has a comparative advantage in slide decks.
That classmate has an absolute advantage in slide decks.
That classmate will always earn more from trade.
That classmate must produce every slide deck for the class.
artifact.ex: That classmate has a comparative advantage in slide decks because the deciding factor is lower opportunity cost. A common mistake is to confuse this with absolute advantage, but being better at everything is not what makes the advantage comparative.

claims: An externality is a cost or benefit from a transaction that falls on a third party who is not part of the exchange.
With a negative externality like pollution, the market produces more than the socially efficient quantity because the price excludes the spillover cost.
Correcting an externality means making decision-makers face the costs or benefits the market boundary leaves out.

op: Some of the cost of a transaction is paid by a bystander.
The buyer and seller both bear the full cost of their trade.
Only the firm making the choice pays every cost created by it.
A price change happens before the trade takes place.
artifact.ex: The first option fits because a cost from the exchange lands on someone outside the exchange. The other choices describe costs staying inside the trade, which is not an externality under the claim.

artifact.q: When a negative externality exists, what is the typical market outcome compared to the socially efficient quantity?
op: The market produces the socially efficient quantity because the price incorporates the spill-on
The market produces more than the socially efficient quantity because the price excludes the sp
The market produces less than the socially efficient quantity because the price includes the sp
The market produces the socially efficient quantity because the price incorporates the sp
artifact.ex: The market produces more than the socially efficient quantity because the price excludes the spillover cost. The most plausible misconception is that the market outcome is always the socially efficient quantity, which is incorrect when negative externalities are present.

claims: A monopoly is a market with a single seller of a product that has no close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry.
Unlike a price-taking competitive firm, a monopoly is a price maker: it can raise price by restricting the quantity it sells.
Because it produces less and charges more than a competitive market, a monopoly creates deadweight loss.

artifact.q: What is a monopoly able to do differently from a price-taking competitive firm?
op: Raise price by restricting the quantity it sells
Keep price fixed by selling whatever amount buyers want
Avoid all losses because it faces no rivals
Set price only by matching the average firm in the market
artifact.ex: Correct: it sells less and charges more than a competitive market, creating deadweight loss. That is not the same as simply being a big seller.

artifact.q: What economic consequence arises when a single seller produces less and charges a higher price than a competitive market?
op: Deadweight loss
Absolute advantage
Comparative advantage
Private cost
artifact.ex: Because it produces less and charges more than a competitive market, a monopoly creates deadweight loss.

claims: By the law of supply, a higher price raises the quantity producers are willing to supply, so the supply curve slopes upward.
A change in the good's own price moves along the supply curve, while a change in input costs or technology shifts the whole curve.
Quantity supplied is a flow per period, not a fixed stock.

artifact.q: Which factor causes the entire supply curve to shift?
op: A change in the good's own price
B a change in input costs or technology
C a change in quantity supplied
D a change in the good's stock
artifact.ex: B is correct. A change in input costs or technology shifts the whole curve. Quantity supplied is a flow per period, not a fixed stock.

artifact.q: A farmer says, “I supply 50 bushels of corn.” Which statement fits the idea of quantity supplied?
op: It is a flow measured over a period
It is a fixed stock sitting in storage
It is the market price of corn
It is the farmer's technology level
artifact.ex: It is a flow measured over a period because quantity supplied is described as a per-period amount. The common mistake is to treat it like a stock, but the claim distinguishes flow from fixed stock.
